titre: The Constitutional Council Discovers Itself as Guardian of Liberties
accroche: In 1971, a refused association pushes the government to lock down declarations. The Constitutional Council invents review for fundamental rights.
contenu_vulgarise:
Summer 1970, Paris. The Maoist newspaper *La Cause du Peuple* is repeatedly banned for its calls to revolutionary violence, and the organization it came from, the Gauche prolétarienne, is dissolved in May. To keep distributing it without its sellers being harassed, its supporters register an association, Les Amis de la Cause du Peuple, backed notably by Simone de Beauvoir. Interior Minister Raymond Marcellin sees in it the disguised reconstitution of the dissolved movement. The Paris police prefect refuses to issue the receipt for the declaration.

## A law to cover a refusal already made

That refusal has no legal basis at the time: since the law of July 1, 1901, an association is formed by simple declaration, without any prior authorization of any kind. To regularize the practice, the government has a bill passed amending articles 5 and 7 of that law, which would subject the validity of an association to prior judicial review. In the Senate, Senator Pierre Marcilhacy opposes it and gets a motion to reject adopted, on June 28, 1971, by 129 votes to 104. The National Assembly, for its part, keeps the text and passes it on June 30.

The President of the Senate, Alain Poher, then refers the matter to the Constitutional Council under Article 61 of the Constitution, on July 1, 1971, seventy years to the day after the law he is defending. Until then, the Council had ruled only on the regularity of how the public authorities operated in relation to one another, never on the conformity of a law with individual rights.

## A recital that changes the nature of the Council

On July 16, 1971, the Council hands down its decision. It holds that freedom of association is “amongst the fundamental principles recognised under the laws of the Republic and solemnly reaffirmed in the preamble to the Constitution,” and strikes down the article establishing prior review. The reasoning matters as much as the result: by basing its decision on the preamble of the 1958 Constitution (which refers to the 1789 Declaration and the 1946 preamble), the Council gives binding force, for the first time, to texts previously regarded as mere statements of intent. What legal scholars would call the “constitutional bloc” (*bloc de constitutionnalité*) is born.

The affair that triggered the decision, an association for selling a banned newspaper, quickly fades from memory. What remains is the tool the Council has just given itself without naming it: the power to strike down a law no longer merely because it encroaches on the competences of another body, but because it infringes a right. Three years later, in 1974, a constitutional revision would open referrals to sixty members of Parliament, allowing this brand-new power to be exercised far more often than a handful of institutional authorities would ever have called on it.

repere.texte: On July 1, 1971 (seventy years to the day after the law it amends), the President of the Senate, Alain Poher, refers the matter to the Constitutional Council. Fifteen days later, on July 16, the Council strikes down the law, relying for the first time on the preamble to the Constitution.
repere.source: Decision no. 71-44 DC of July 16, 1971, Constitutional Council

carte.punch: A refused association in 1970, and the Constitutional Council becomes guardian of liberties.
carte.idee: In 1971, the government wants to subject associations to prior review, after refusing to register one. Referred by the President of the Senate, the Constitutional Council strikes down the law, relying for the first time on the preamble to the Constitution.

quiz.question: Why is the Constitutional Council's decision of July 16, 1971 considered a turning point?
choix: Because it annuls for the first time a law contrary to the very text of the Constitution
Because it gives the National Assembly the last word over the Senate
Because it authorizes, for the first time, prior judicial review of associations
Because it bases, for the first time, the striking down of a law on the preamble to the Constitution
quiz.explication: Until then the Council reviewed only the division of competences among the public authorities. By relying on the preamble (which refers to the 1789 Declaration and the 1946 preamble) to strike down the law, it gives those texts unprecedented binding force, and invents for itself a role as guardian of fundamental rights that no provision explicitly gave it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who, in practice, refuses to issue the declaration receipt to the association Les Amis de la Cause du Peuple?
choix: The President of the Senate, who would later refer the matter to the Constitutional Council
The Minister of Justice, responsible for validating new associations
The Paris police prefect, who suspects a disguised reconstitution
The Constitutional Council, referred to directly by the government
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Interior Minister Raymond Marcellin saw in it the disguised reconstitution of the Gauche prolétarienne, but it is the police prefect who concretely refuses the receipt, with no legal basis at that point.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens in the Senate on June 28, 1971, before the Council is seized?
choix: The Senate adopts, by 129 votes to 104, a motion to reject the bill brought by Senator Marcilhacy
The Senate passes the bill in the same terms as the National Assembly
The Senate itself refers the matter directly to the Constitutional Council
The Senate proposes a new wording of articles 5 and 7 of the 1901 law
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Senator Pierre Marcilhacy opposes the bill and gets a motion to reject adopted, 129 votes to 104, on June 28, 1971. The National Assembly, for its part, keeps the text and passes it two days later, on June 30.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the constitutional revision of 1974 concretely change?
choix: It gives the Constitutional Council the power to annul a law
It formally incorporates the 1789 Declaration into the text of the Constitution
It transfers to the Senate alone the power to refer matters to the Constitutional Council
It opens referrals to the Constitutional Council to sixty members of Parliament
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Before 1974, only a few institutional authorities could refer matters to the Council. The 1974 revision opens that right to sixty members of Parliament, multiplying the occasions to exercise the review invented in 1971.
